title: The Toughest Little Animal
passage: The honey badger may be small, but it is one of the bravest animals in Africa.
It is about the size of a medium dog, with black fur and a white stripe on its back.
Its skin is thick and loose, like a coat that is a size too big.
If a lion grabs it, the honey badger can twist around inside its skin and bite back!
Honey badgers eat almost anything, from insects and frogs to snakes and scorpions.
Some can even survive a bite from a venomous snake.
As their name suggests, they love honey and the baby bees inside a hive.
They use their long, sharp claws to tear the hive open.
The angry bees sting them, but their thick skin protects them.
Honey badgers are also very clever.

title: Thandi Learns to Surf
passage: During the December holidays, Thandi had her first surfing lesson at Muizenberg Beach.
Her instructor, Kyle, gave her a thick wetsuit and a big foam surfboard.

Thandi learnt to paddle with her arms and then jump up quickly onto her feet.
She had to keep her knees bent and her arms out for balance.
After ten practice runs, they carried the board into the shallow water.
Kyle held the back of the board while they waited for a small wave.
"Paddle, paddle, paddle!" he shouted as the wave arrived.
Thandi paddled hard and tried to stand up, but she wobbled and fell off with a splash.
She tried again and again, swallowing plenty of salty water.
On her ninth try, she finally stood up and rode the wave all the way to the beach.

title: Life on the Space Station
passage: High above the Earth, a huge spacecraft called the International Space Station circles our planet.
It travels so fast that it goes around the whole Earth in about ninety minutes.
That means the astronauts on board see about sixteen sunrises every day!
Up to seven astronauts from different countries live and work there together.
Because there is almost no gravity, everything floats.
The astronauts sleep in sleeping bags tied to the walls so they don't drift around.
They have to exercise for about two hours every day.
Without exercise, their muscles and bones would become weak.
Water is so precious that they even clean and recycle their sweat and urine into drinking water!
The astronauts also do science experiments that can't be done on Earth.
Through the windows, they can see storms, cities lit up at night and the thin blue line of our atmosphere.
Many astronauts say that seeing Earth from space changed how they think about our planet.
It looks small and beautiful, with no borders between countries.

title: The Message in a Bottle
passage: While walking along the beach with her dog, Lerato spotted something shiny in the seaweed.
It was an old green bottle with a cork in the top.
Inside, she could see a rolled-up piece of paper.
Carefully, she pulled out the cork and shook the paper into her hand.
The letter was written in neat handwriting and dated ten years ago!
"My name is Emma, and I am nine years old," it said. "I live in Australia."
"I threw this bottle into the sea to see how far it would travel."
At the bottom was an address and a request to write back.
Lerato raced home to show her parents.
Together they looked at a map and traced the long journey across the Indian Ocean.
That evening, Lerato and her parents wrote a letter and posted it to the address.
Weeks later, a thick envelope with colourful stamps arrived.
Emma was now nineteen and studying to become a marine scientist.
Now the two families write to each other every year.

title: When the Desert Blooms
passage: For most of the year, Namaqualand is a dry and dusty place.

The empty land turns into a carpet of orange, yellow, white and purple.

"Why are they all looking in one direction?" he asked his dad.
Dad explained that the flowers turn their faces towards the sun.
They open in the warm middle of the day and close again when it is cool or cloudy.
That's why it is best to visit between ten in the morning and four in the afternoon.
The seeds of these flowers can lie in the dry ground for years, waiting for rain.

title: Bread from Scratch
passage: On a rainy Sunday, Sipho and his aunt decided to bake bread from scratch.
They mixed flour, salt, warm water and a spoonful of yeast in a big bowl.
Aunt Lindi explained that yeast is a tiny living thing, too small to see.
When it is warm, the yeast eats the sugars in the flour and makes bubbles of gas.
These bubbles make the dough rise and become light and fluffy.
Sipho kneaded the dough for ten minutes, pushing and folding it on the table.
His arms grew tired, but the dough became smooth and stretchy.
They covered the bowl with a cloth and left it in a warm spot.
An hour later, Sipho lifted the cloth and gasped.
The dough had grown to twice its size!
Aunt Lindi shaped it into a loaf and baked it in a hot oven.
Soon the whole house smelt of fresh bread.
When it was ready, she tapped the bottom, and it sounded hollow.
"That means it's cooked through," she said.
They ate warm slices with butter and apricot jam.

title: Die pikkewyne by Boulders
passage: Graad vier het lank uitgesien na hul uitstappie na Boulders-strand naby Simonstad. Die bus het vroeg vertrek, en die kinders het die hele pad gesing. Juffrou Nel het belowe dat hulle 'n baie spesiale voël sou sien.

Toe hulle by die strand aankom, het die kinders hul oë nie geglo nie. Honderde swart-en-wit pikkewyne het op die rotse en in die warm sand gestaan. Party het in die see geswem, en ander het net in die son gelê. Skielik het een pikkewyn sy kop agteroor gegooi en hard begin balk. "Hy klink net soos 'n donkie!" het Thabo gelag.

Die gids het verduidelik dat die Afrikaanse pikkewyn net aan die kus van Suider-Afrika voorkom. Hierdie pikkewyne kan nie vlieg nie, maar hulle is uitstekende swemmers. Hulle gebruik hul vlerke soos roeispane om vinnig deur die water te beweeg. Hulle eet klein vissies soos sardyne en ansjovis, wat hulle onder die water vang. Die pienk kolle bo hul oë help hulle om koel te bly op warm dae.

Ongelukkig word daar elke jaar minder pikkewyne. Mense vang te veel vis in die see, en daarom kry die voëls nie genoeg kos nie. Olie en plastiek in die water maak hulle ook siek. Die gids het gesê dat ons almal kan help deur nooit rommel op die strand te los nie.

Op pad huis toe was die bus heeltemal stil. Elke kind het aan die snaakse pikkewyne gedink. Thabo het besluit dat hy eendag 'n natuurbewaarder wil word. "Dan kan ek help om die pikkewyne te beskerm," het hy trots gesê.

title: Oupa draf die Comrades
passage: Toe Oupa Johan sestig geword het, het hy iets besluit wat almal verbaas het. Hy wou die Comrades-maraton voltooi, een van die bekendste langafstandwedlope in die wêreld. Die wedloop is omtrent negentig kilometer lank, tussen Durban en Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal.

Elke jaar verander die rigting van die wedloop. Die een jaar hardloop die atlete bergop na Pietermaritzburg, en die volgende jaar weer afdraand na Durban. Albei is moeilik, want die pad is vol lang, steil bulte. Die atlete moet binne twaalf uur by die eindstreep wees, anders kry hulle nie 'n medalje nie.

Vir 'n hele jaar het Oupa elke oggend voor sonop gaan oefen. Ek het dikwels saam met hom op my fiets gery en vir hom water gedra. Hy het gesond geëet, vroeg gaan slaap en sy afstande stadig langer gemaak. Somtyds was sy bene so seer dat hy skaars die trappe kon klim.

Op die dag van die wedloop het ons langs die pad gestaan en vir hom gewag. Toe hy verbykom, het ons geskree en hom 'n lemoen aangegee. Hy het moeg gelyk, maar sy oë het geblink. Laat die middag het hy uiteindelik oor die eindstreep gestrompel, net twintig minute voordat die twaalf uur verby was.

Toe die vrywilliger die medalje om sy nek hang, het Oupa soos 'n kind gehuil van blydskap. "Dit is nooit te laat om 'n droom na te jaag nie," het hy vir my gesê. Daardie medalje hang nou by sy voordeur, sodat almal wat inkom dit kan sien. En ek? Ek begin volgende week saam met hom oefen vir 'n pretdraf.

title: Waarheen gaan ons rommel?
passage: Elke Donderdag sit Zanele se gesin 'n groen sak vol ou koerante, bottels en blikkies by die hek. Een oggend wonder sy waarheen die sak eintlik gaan. Haar juffrou reël toe 'n uitstappie na 'n herwinningsaanleg naby die dorp.

By die aanleg ry groot vragmotors vol rommel deur die hekke. Werkers en masjiene sorteer alles op lang lopende bande. Papier gaan na een kant, plastiek na 'n ander, en glas en blik elkeen na hul eie hoop. 'n Sterk magneet trek selfs die staalblikkies uit die hoop!

Die gids wys hulle hoe ou papier weer nuwe papier word. Eers word dit in water geweek totdat dit 'n dik pap vorm. Die ink word uitgewas, en die pap word op lang skerms uitgesprei om droog te word. Warm rollers druk dit dan plat, en dit word groot rolle nuwe papier. Hierdie papier word later eierkartonne, toiletpapier of selfs nuwe koerante.
"Elke ton papier wat ons herwin, spaar baie bome en water," verduidelik die gids. "Dit hou ook rommel uit die stortingsterrein, waar dit baie jare lank sou lê."

Op pad terug skool toe maak Zanele 'n plan. Sy gaan 'n herwinningshoek in hul klaskamer begin, met aparte houers vir papier, plastiek en blik. Die klas besluit om elke maand te tel hoeveel sakke hulle versamel. Die skoolhoof belowe 'n pizzapartytjie vir die klas wat teen die einde van die jaar die meeste herwin het. Zanele glimlag, want sy weet hul klas gaan hard werk. Klein dade, glo sy, kan saam 'n groot verskil maak.

title: Die rooibosplaas
passage: In die vakansie gaan kuier Anika by haar tante op 'n rooibosplaas in die Sederberge. Sy het nog altyd rooibostee gedrink, maar nooit geweet waar dit vandaan kom nie.

Tant Elsa verduidelik dat rooibos 'n fynbosplantjie is wat net in hierdie deel van die Wes-Kaap natuurlik groei. Die plant het fyn, naaldagtige blaartjies en diep wortels wat water ver onder die grond vind. Lank gelede het die Khoi-mense al die blare gepluk en tee daarvan gemaak.

Anika help die werkers om die groen takkies met sekels af te sny. Die takkies word dan fyngekap en natgemaak. Daarna word dit in lang rye op die grond uitgepak en met 'n hark gekneus. Dan gebeur daar iets wonderliks. In die warm son verander die groen blaartjies stadig na 'n diep rooibruin kleur. Dit is ook wanneer die tee sy soet, lekker geur kry.

Die tee word in die son gedroog en daarna in sakke gepak. Van die plaas word dit na fabrieke gestuur, waar dit in teesakkies verpak word. Vandag drink mense regoor die wêreld rooibos. "Rooibos het geen kafeïen nie, dus kan selfs kinders dit saans drink," sê Tant Elsa.

Die laaste aand sit Anika en haar tante op die stoep met 'n warm koppie tee. Die son sak agter die rotse, wat net so rooi soos die tee gloei. Anika vat 'n slukkie en glimlag. Van nou af sal elke koppie rooibos haar aan hierdie plaas laat dink. Sy besluit om 'n sakkie van die plaas se tee vir haar juffrou te neem.

title: Hoe genees 'n skaafplek?
passage: Tijan het van sy skaatsplank afgeval en sy knie oopgeskaaf. Hy het gehuil, want dit het gebrand en effens gebloei. Ma het die skaafplek met skoon water gewas en 'n pleister daarop gesit.

"Hoe weet my knie hoe om gesond te word?" wou Tijan later weet. Ma het haar selfoon uitgehaal en saam met hom oor die liggaam gelees. Hulle het geleer dat bloed klein deeltjies bevat wat bloedplaatjies genoem word. Sodra jy jouself sny, haas die bloedplaatjies hulle na die wond. Hulle klou aan mekaar vas en vorm 'n prop wat die bloeding stop.

Die prop word hard en droog, en dit word 'n kors. Die kors is soos 'n dak wat die wond beskerm terwyl nuwe vel daaronder groei. Intussen stuur die liggaam wit bloedselle na die plek. Hulle werk soos klein soldate wat kieme aanval, sodat die wond nie besmet raak nie.

Na 'n week het die kors begin jeuk. Tijan wou dit baie graag afkrap, maar Ma het hom gewaarsku. "As jy die kors afkrap, maak jy die wond weer oop, en dit kan 'n merk los," het sy gesê. Dus het Tijan geduldig gewag.

Twee weke later het die kors vanself afgeval. Daaronder was pienk, nuwe vel. Tijan was verbaas dat sy liggaam alles self reggemaak het. "My lyf is soos 'n slim fabriek," het hy gesê. Nou dra hy altyd kniekussings wanneer hy skaatsplank ry. Hy het geleer dat dit beter is om 'n val te voorkom as om 'n wond te genees.

title: Waarom verander die maan?
passage: Elke aand voor slaaptyd kyk Lebo by haar kamervenster uit na die maan. Sy het opgelet dat die maan elke aand 'n bietjie anders lyk. Soms is dit 'n dun, blink sekel, en soms is dit 'n groot, ronde bal.

Op 'n dag vra sy vir haar oupa waarom die maan sy vorm verander. Oupa haal 'n flits en 'n lemoen uit die kombuis. Hy trek die gordyne toe sodat die kamer donker is. "Die flits is die son, en die lemoen is die maan," verduidelik hy. "Jou kop is die aarde."

Oupa laat die flits op die lemoen skyn terwyl hy die lemoen stadig om Lebo se kop beweeg. Lebo sien hoe die lig op die lemoen verander. Wanneer die lemoen tussen haar en die flits is, kan sy net die donker kant sien. Dit is soos die nuwemaan, wanneer ons die maan glad nie kan sien nie. Wanneer die lemoen agter haar kop is, is die hele kant wat na haar kyk helder. Dit is volmaan.

"Die maan maak nie sy eie lig nie," sê Oupa. "Dit weerkaats die lig van die son, en dit neem omtrent 'n maand om een keer om die aarde te draai." Die verskillende vorms word die fases van die maan genoem.

Van daardie aand af hou Lebo 'n maanboek. Elke aand teken sy presies hoe die maan lyk. Na 'n maand het sy al die fases in haar boek. Sy neem dit skool toe en wys dit trots vir haar klas. Juffrou is so beïndruk dat sy dit teen die muur opplak.

title: Verdwaal in die mis
passage: Ruben en sy ouer suster Mia was saam met hul pa op 'n staptog in die Drakensberg. Die oggend was helder, en hulle kon kilometers ver oor die pieke sien. Teen middagete het Pa vorentoe gaan kyk of die pad verder oop was, terwyl die kinders by die rugsakke gewag het.

Skielik het 'n dik, grys mis oor die berg gerol. Binne minute kon Ruben skaars sy eie hande sien. "Pa!" het hy geroep, maar net sy eie stem het teruggeëggo. Hy wou begin hardloop om Pa te soek, maar Mia het sy arm gegryp.

"Onthou wat Pa ons geleer het," het sy kalm gesê. "As jy verdwaal, bly waar jy is, sodat mense jou kan kry." Hulle het teen 'n groot rots gaan sit en hul warm baadjies aangetrek. Mia het die fluitjie uit haar rugsak gehaal en drie kort, harde fluitjies geblaas. Drie fluitjies beteken dat iemand hulp nodig het.

Hulle het gewag en elke paar minute weer geblaas. Dit het koud en stil geword, en Ruben se hart het vinnig geklop. Toe, uit die mis, het hulle 'n antwoord gehoor: twee fluitjies! Kort daarna het Pa se helderrooi baadjie deur die grys mis verskyn.

Pa het albei styf vasgedruk. "Julle het presies die regte ding gedoen," het hy gesê. "Baie mense raak paniekerig en loop nog verder weg." Toe die mis 'n uur later oplig, het hulle gesien dat die rand van 'n krans net 'n paar meter van hul rots af was. Ruben het gesluk. Van daardie dag af dra hy altyd 'n fluitjie wanneer hy gaan stap.

title: Die vleiland
passage: Anke se klas gaan op 'n uitstappie na 'n vleiland naby hul dorp. Sy het verwag dat dit net 'n modderige, vervelige plek gaan wees. Maar sodra hulle op die houtbrug stap, verander sy van plan.

Oral om hulle groei lang riete en biesies wat saggies in die wind wieg. Honderde voëls roep, fluit en plas in die vlak water. Die gids wys vir hulle 'n grys reier en 'n klein, bont ysvoël. Uit die riete kom die harde, snaakse geluid van paddas.

"'n Vleiland is soos 'n reuse-spons," verduidelik die gids. "Wanneer dit baie reën, suig dit die water op en keer dat die dorp oorstroom. In droë tye laat dit die water stadig los, sodat die riviere nie opdroog nie." Die plante in die vleiland maak ook die water skoon deur vuilheid uit te filtreer.

Ongelukkig word baie vleilande in Suid-Afrika vernietig. Mense bou huise en paaie daarop, of hulle gooi rommel in die water. Wanneer 'n vleiland verdwyn, verloor die voëls, paddas en visse hul huis. Die dorp kry ook meer oorstromings en vuiler water.

Voor hulle huis toe gaan, help die klas om plastiek uit die riete te haal. Anke vind 'n ou koeldrankbottel en drie plastieksakke. Op die bus terug sit sy stil en dink. Sy het nie geweet dat 'n modderige plek so belangrik kan wees nie. Toe hulle by die skool aankom, vra sy vir haar juffrou of die klas 'n plakkaat oor die beskerming van vleilande kan maak. title: Maya and the Night Sky
passage: Maya's family went camping in the Karoo during the school holidays. Far away from the bright lights of the city, the night sky looked completely different. As soon as the sun set, thousands of stars began to twinkle above their tent.

Maya lay on a blanket next to her grandfather and stared upwards in amazement. "I have never seen so many stars before!" she whispered. Grandpa smiled and pointed at a long, cloudy band of light stretching across the sky. "That is the Milky Way," he explained. "It is our galaxy, and it contains billions of stars, including our own Sun."

Next, Grandpa showed her four bright stars in the shape of a kite. This is the Southern Cross, which can only be seen properly from the southern half of the world. Two very bright stars nearby, called the Pointers, lead the way to it. Long ago, sailors and travellers used these stars to find the direction of south at night.

Later, a round yellow moon rose slowly over the hills. Maya was surprised to learn that the Moon does not make any light of its own. Instead, it reflects the light of the Sun, just like a mirror. Grandpa also told her that the stars are actually enormous suns, but they are so far away that they look like tiny dots.

That night, Maya fell asleep dreaming about rockets and faraway planets. The next morning she asked her parents for a telescope for her birthday. "One day," she said confidently, "I am going to be an astronaut!"

title: The Sardine Run
passage: Every winter, one of the greatest wildlife shows on Earth takes place along the east coast of South Africa. It is called the Sardine Run. Between May and July, huge shoals of tiny silver sardines swim north along the coast of KwaZulu-Natal. Some shoals are several kilometres long and can be seen from the air as dark patches in the water.

Scientists believe the sardines follow a band of cool water that flows up the coast in winter. For the sardines, it is a dangerous journey. Thousands of dolphins, sharks, seals and birds follow them, ready for a feast.

The common dolphins are clever hunters. They work together to herd the sardines into a tight ball near the surface. This is called a bait ball. Then the dolphins take turns darting through it to feed. From above, Cape gannets fold back their wings and dive into the water like arrows. They can plunge up to ten metres deep to catch their prey.

Divers and photographers travel from all over the world to see this amazing sight. Local fishermen also wait on the beaches with nets. When a shoal comes close to the shore, people rush into the shallow water to scoop up sardines in buckets.

title: The Wheelchair Basketball Match
passage: When Karabo's cousin Sipho invited him to watch a basketball match, Karabo expected an ordinary game. But when he arrived at the sports hall, all the players were in wheelchairs. Sipho had been born with legs that didn't work, but that had never stopped him.

The wheelchairs were not like normal ones. They were light and low, with wheels that slanted inwards so they could turn quickly without tipping over. Players pushed the wheels with their hands and had to bounce the ball at the same time. The rules were almost the same as in ordinary basketball.

The game was fast and exciting. Chairs crashed into each other with loud bangs, and sometimes a player tipped right over. Each time, they pushed themselves back up and carried on playing. Sipho was the team's best shooter. With seconds left, he spun his chair around, aimed and threw the ball high into the air.
The whole hall held its breath as the ball swirled around the rim. Then it dropped through the net, and the crowd erupted with cheers. Sipho's team had won by two points!

After the match, Sipho let Karabo try a spare wheelchair. It was much harder than it looked. Within minutes his arms were burning, and he could barely steer in a straight line. "How do you do this for a whole game?" he gasped. Sipho laughed. "Practice, practice and more practice." Karabo left the hall with a new respect for his cousin and a new favourite sport.

title: The Time Capsule
passage: When Riverside Primary celebrated its hundredth birthday, the principal made an exciting announcement. Fifty years earlier, pupils had buried a time capsule under the big oak tree on the field. Now it was time to dig it up.

The whole school gathered around as two gardeners carefully dug into the hard ground. After an hour, a spade struck metal. Slowly, they lifted out a rusty tin box, its lid sealed with thick wax. Nadia, who was in Grade 5, was chosen to help open it. Her hands shook with excitement as she pulled off the lid.

Inside were treasures from a very different time. There was a black-and-white photo of a class wearing long socks and old-fashioned school hats. There was a newspaper that had cost only two cents, and a comic with a torn cover. A small cassette tape was labelled "Our favourite songs". Nobody in Nadia's class had ever seen one before!

At the bottom was a letter written by the children of long ago. "We wonder if you still have to learn your times tables," it said. "We wonder if cars can fly yet, and if everyone has a robot to do their homework." The whole school burst out laughing.

That afternoon, Nadia's class decided to make a new time capsule. They added a class photo, a drawing of a tablet, a list of their favourite games and a letter to the future. On the envelope, Nadia wrote: "Do not open for fifty years." She wondered what the children of the future would think of them.

title: After the Fire
passage: One summer night, Liam watched an orange glow on the mountain behind his home in Cape Town. A veld fire was burning through the fynbos. Firefighters and helicopters worked through the night to keep it away from the houses.

A week later, Liam and his father walked up the burnt mountainside. Everything was black, and the air still smelt of smoke. "It's so sad," said Liam. "Everything is dead." His father shook his head. "Not everything. Fynbos actually needs fire to stay healthy."

He explained that many fynbos plants only release their seeds after a fire. Some seeds need the heat of the flames to crack open. Others are woken up by chemicals in the smoke. The ash also acts like fertiliser, adding food to the soil. Without a fire every ten to twenty years, the old bushes grow too thick, and new plants can't grow.

A few months later, they climbed the mountain again. Liam couldn't believe his eyes. Bright green shoots were pushing up through the black soil. Fire lilies, with their bright red flowers, bloomed everywhere. Sunbirds and bees were busy visiting the flowers.

However, his father warned that fires started by people are dangerous. If fires happen too often, the young plants don't have time to grow up and make seeds. That is why we must never throw away burning matches or leave campfires unattended. Liam realised that nature is cleverer than he had thought. Even after a disaster, it knows how to heal itself.

title: Making a Rainbow
passage: After a sudden summer storm, a huge rainbow stretched across the sky above Ayesha's house. Her little brother Zain asked where rainbows come from. Ayesha wasn't sure, so she decided to find out.

At the library, she found a book about light. It explained that sunlight looks white, but it is actually made up of many colours mixed together. When sunlight passes through a raindrop, the light bends. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the colours spread out. The raindrop acts like a tiny prism.

The book also explained that rainbows always have the same order of colours. Red is on the outside, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Some people remember the order with the name "Roy G. Biv", using the first letter of each colour. To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you.

Ayesha wanted to show Zain how it works. On a sunny morning, she filled a glass with water and put it on the windowsill. She placed a sheet of white paper on the floor below it. Slowly, she moved the glass until the sunlight shone through it. Suddenly, a small rainbow appeared on the paper!

Zain clapped his hands and tried to catch the colours. Then they went outside and sprayed a fine mist from the hosepipe, with their backs to the sun. Another rainbow shimmered in the air. "Now I can make a rainbow whenever I want," laughed Zain.

title: From Bean to Bar
passage: When Tumi bit into her chocolate bar, she suddenly wondered where chocolate actually comes from. She was surprised to learn that it starts as a seed growing on a tree.

Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows in hot, rainy places near the equator. More than half of the world's cacao comes from two countries in West Africa: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. The seeds, called cocoa beans, grow inside large pods that sprout straight from the tree trunk. When the pods are ripe, they turn yellow, orange or red.

Farmers cut the pods open with a machete and scoop out the beans, which are covered in a sweet white pulp. The beans are left to ferment under banana leaves for about a week. This is when they begin to develop their chocolatey flavour. Then they are spread out in the sun to dry.

The dried beans are shipped to factories all over the world. There, they are roasted, cracked open and ground into a thick, dark paste. Sugar, milk and cocoa butter are mixed in to make the smooth chocolate that we know. Surprisingly, raw cocoa beans taste very bitter, not sweet at all!

Tumi also learnt that many cacao farmers earn very little money. Some chocolate has a special label showing that the farmers were paid fairly. The next time Tumi went to the shop with her mom, she looked for that label. Her chocolate tasted even sweeter, knowing that the farmers had been treated fairly.

title: The Secret Life of Bones
passage: When Leo broke his wrist falling off a trampoline, he spent six weeks in a cast. During that time, he became curious about the bones inside his body.

He learnt that an adult's skeleton has 206 bones. Amazingly, a baby is born with around 300! As babies grow, some of their bones slowly join together. The smallest bone is in your ear and is about the size of a grain of rice. The longest is the thigh bone, which runs from your hip to your knee.

Many people think bones are dry and dead, like sticks. In fact, bones are alive. They have blood flowing through them, and they can grow and repair themselves. Inside some bones is a soft, jelly-like material called marrow. Marrow makes millions of new blood cells every second.

To stay strong, bones need calcium, which is found in milk, cheese, yoghurt and green vegetables. Bones also need exercise. When you run, jump or dance, your bones become thicker and stronger. Sunlight helps too, because it helps your body make vitamin D, which your body needs to use calcium.

When Leo's cast finally came off, his wrist looked thin and weak. The doctor said this was normal and gave him exercises to do. Leo squeezed a soft ball every day and drank a glass of milk with every meal. Within a month, his wrist was as strong as before. "My bones are cleverer than I thought," said Leo. He still bounces on the trampoline, but a little more carefully now.

title: Tumelo the Orphan Rhino
passage: One morning, rangers in the Kruger National Park found a baby rhino standing alone beside a waterhole. It was only a few weeks old, and its mother was nowhere to be seen. Without her milk and protection, the little calf would not survive.

The rangers carefully loaded the calf onto a truck and drove it to a rhino orphanage. There, a team of carers named him Tumelo, which means "faith" in Setswana. Tumelo was frightened and cried with a high-pitched squeak. To calm him, one carer stayed with him day and night, just as his mother would have.

Baby rhinos drink a lot of milk. Tumelo needed a special milk mixture from a giant bottle every three hours. Within a few weeks, he was following his carers everywhere, like a large, grey puppy. He loved rolling in mud, which protects a rhino's skin from the sun and insects.

Rhinos are in danger because some people hunt them illegally for their horns. Their horns are made of keratin, the same material as our hair and fingernails. The carers hope that one day there will be enough safe places for all rhinos to live freely.

After three years, Tumelo was big and strong enough to return to the wild. On the day of his release, the carers watched with tears in their eyes as he trotted into the bush. Rangers still watch over him from a distance. Tumelo, whose name means faith, has shown that there is still hope for rhinos.

title: Lost in the Maize Maze
passage: For Nomsa's birthday, her family visited a giant maize maze on a farm outside Pretoria. The farmer had cut narrow paths through a field of maize plants that were taller than any adult. "The first team to reach the tower in the middle wins a prize," he announced.

Nomsa and her cousin Thabo set off confidently. At first it was fun, turning left and right between the rustling green walls. But after twenty minutes, they had walked past the same scarecrow three times. "We're going around in circles," groaned Thabo.

Nomsa remembered something she had read in a book about mazes. "If you keep one hand touching the wall and never let go, you'll eventually find your way," she said. It might not be the shortest route, but it would stop them from getting completely lost. They chose the right-hand wall and set off again, trailing their fingers along the leaves.

The path twisted and turned through dead ends and long corners. Twice they had to walk back the way they had come. Thabo wanted to give up, but Nomsa kept her hand firmly on the wall. At last, they turned a corner and saw the wooden tower rising above the maize.

They climbed to the top, panting and laughing. From up there, they could see the whole maze spread out below them like a green puzzle. They weren't the first team, but the farmer gave them a prize anyway: two ice-cold cooldrinks for the cleverest strategy. "Next year," said Thabo, "I'm bringing that book!"

passage: Het jy al ooit gewonder waar die water vandaan kom wat so maklik uit jou kraan loop? Dit lyk dalk asof daar altyd genoeg sal wees, maar in Suid-Afrika is water eintlik baie skaars. Die meeste water in 'n huis word in die badkamer gebruik, en dit is juis daar waar jy die grootste verskil kan maak. Wie het nou eintlik 'n vol bad nodig as 'n vinnige stort net so lekker is? Probeer om jou stort korter as vyf minute te hou, en draai die kraan toe terwyl jy jou tande borsel. title: Klein diertjies, groot werk
passage: Wanneer jy 'n by sien, dink jy waarskynlik eerste aan 'n pynlike steek. Baie mense is bang vir bye en probeer hulle so gou moontlik wegjaag. Tog is hierdie klein insekte van die belangrikste diere op ons planeet. Sonder bye sou ons kosborde baie leër en vervelig lyk.

title: Kos is kosbaar
passage: Dink aan die laaste keer toe jy kos in die asblik gegooi het. Miskien was dit 'n halwe toebroodjie, 'n brood wat te lank gestaan het, of groente wat in die yskas verlep het. Dit lyk dalk na 'n klein ding, maar al daardie klein bietjies tel vinnig op.

title: Krag uit die son
passage: Tydens beurtkrag het baie Suid-Afrikaanse gesinne sonpanele op hul dakke laat installeer. Jy het dalk al die blink, donkerblou panele op huise, skole en selfs by verkeersligte gesien. Maar hoe verander 'n plat stuk glas sonlig in elektrisiteit wat 'n yskas kan laat werk?

title: Why Sleep Matters
passage: Do you ever beg your parents for "just five more minutes" when it is time for bed? Most children would much rather stay up late, watching television or playing games with their brothers and sisters. However, scientists have discovered that sleep is one of the most important things you can do for your body and your brain.

While you are fast asleep, your body is actually very busy. It repairs tired muscles, fights off germs and even helps you grow taller. Your brain sorts through everything you learnt during the day and stores the important parts in your memory, almost like a librarian packing books onto the right shelves. That is why a good night's sleep before a test is far more useful than staying up late to study.

How much sleep do you really need? Doctors say that children between six and twelve years old should get between nine and twelve hours every night. Without enough rest, you may feel grumpy, find it hard to concentrate in class and even get sick more often.

Luckily, there are a few simple habits that can help you fall asleep more easily. Try to go to bed at the same time every night, even on weekends, so that your body gets used to a routine. Switch off phones, tablets and televisions at least an hour before bedtime, because the bright light from screens tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime. Instead, read a book, take a warm bath or listen to quiet music. Keep your bedroom cool, dark and tidy, and avoid sugary snacks or fizzy drinks late in the evening. Plenty of exercise and fresh air during the day will also make you pleasantly tired by the time the sun goes down.

So the next time you feel like arguing about bedtime, remember what is happening inside your body while you sleep. Sleep is not a waste of time at all. It is your secret weapon for a happy, healthy and successful day!

title: How Does the Internet Reach You?
passage: Every time you watch a video, send a message or search for homework help, information zooms around the world in less than a second. But have you ever wondered how it actually travels? Most people imagine that the internet floats through the air, but the truth is far more surprising.

Almost all of the world's internet traffic travels through cables lying on the bottom of the ocean. These undersea cables stretch for thousands of kilometres between continents. South Africa is connected to Europe, Asia and the Americas by several of these cables, which come ashore at places like Melkbosstrand and Mtunzini. Inside each cable are hair-thin strands of glass called optical fibres. Information travels through them as flashes of light.

When you send a photo to a friend, your device breaks it into thousands of tiny pieces called packets. Each packet is labelled with the address of where it must go, a little like a letter in the post. The packets may travel along different routes, speeding through cables, cell towers and huge buildings full of computers called data centres. When they arrive, your friend's phone puts the pieces back together in the right order, and the photo appears. All of this usually happens in the blink of an eye.

The system works well, but it is not perfect. Sometimes a ship's anchor or an underwater landslide damages a cable. When that happens, the internet in whole countries can become slow for weeks until special repair ships fix it. Engineers keep building new cables so that there are always other routes if one breaks.

The next time a web page loads in a flash, spare a thought for the long journey that information has made. It may have raced under oceans, past sleeping whales and through deep valleys on the sea floor. The internet may feel like magic, but it is really the result of clever engineering and teamwork between countries. Understanding how it works helps us to appreciate it, and perhaps one day you could help to build the next part of it!

title: The Truth About Sugar
passage: Sweets, fizzy drinks, biscuits and ice cream: most of us love sugary treats. There is nothing wrong with enjoying them now and then. The problem is that sugar is hiding in many foods where we least expect it, and most of us eat far more than our bodies need.

Our bodies do need some sugar, because it gives us energy. However, the natural sugar found in fruit comes packed with fibre, vitamins and water, which slow down how fast it enters the blood. Added sugar, on the other hand, is poured into food during cooking or in factories. It gives a quick burst of energy, often followed by a slump that can leave you tired, grumpy and hungry again.

Too much added sugar can harm your health in several ways. The bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar and make acid that eats holes in your teeth. Eating lots of sugar over many years can also lead to weight gain and illnesses such as type 2 diabetes. Health experts recommend that children eat no more than about six teaspoons of added sugar a day. Yet a single can of fizzy drink can contain around eight!

The good news is that small changes make a big difference. Swap fizzy drinks for water, and try adding slices of lemon or mint for flavour. Choose a piece of fruit instead of a chocolate bar. Learn to read food labels, because sugar has many sneaky names, such as glucose, sucrose and corn syrup. You may be surprised to find it in tomato sauce, bread and even so-called "healthy" breakfast cereals.

Nobody is saying you must never eat a sweet again. Birthday cake and the occasional ice cream are part of life's pleasures. The secret is balance. When sugary treats are just that, treats, your body gets the energy it needs from healthy food, and your teeth stay strong. Next time you reach for a sugary snack, ask yourself: "Is this a treat, or has it become a habit?" Your future self will thank you.

title: A Memory Like an Elephant
passage: People often say that "an elephant never forgets". For a long time, this was just a saying. Today, scientists who study elephants in the wild have discovered that it is surprisingly close to the truth. African elephants have some of the most remarkable memories in the animal kingdom.

An elephant's brain is the largest of any land animal, weighing around five kilograms. Elephants live in family groups called herds, which are led by the oldest and wisest female, known as the matriarch. The matriarch remembers where to find water and food, even in places the herd hasn't visited for many years. During a terrible drought in Tanzania, researchers noticed that herds led by older matriarchs, who remembered an earlier drought, survived much better. Their memories quite literally saved lives.

Elephants also remember other elephants and people. They can recognise the calls of family members they have not seen for years. Studies in Kenya showed that elephants can even tell the difference between people from groups that have threatened them in the past and those who have not. They do this by smell and by the sound of people's voices.

Their memories are closely linked to their feelings. Elephants are known to mourn their dead. They sometimes stand quietly around the body of a family member, gently touching it with their trunks. Years later, some herds pause when they pass the bones of a relative, as if they are remembering. Elephant calves that lose their mothers can carry their sadness for a long time, which is why orphanages give them loving human carers.

Sadly, elephants face many dangers today, from poaching to losing their homes as towns and farms grow. When an old matriarch dies, her herd loses a lifetime of knowledge. This is one more reason why protecting elephants, especially the older ones, is so important. The next time someone says you have "a memory like an elephant", take it as a compliment. After all, it is one of the most powerful minds in the natural world.

title: A Traffic Jam in Space
passage: When you look up at the night sky, it seems calm and empty. But hundreds of kilometres above your head, a huge traffic jam is growing. Around our planet, millions of pieces of space junk are racing along at incredible speeds.

Space junk is anything people have sent into space that is no longer useful. It includes old satellites that have stopped working, used rocket parts, and even a glove and a spatula that astronauts accidentally let go of! Most pieces are tiny, like flecks of paint, but thousands are bigger than a tennis ball.

The problem is speed. In orbit, space junk can travel at around 28 000 kilometres an hour, many times faster than a bullet. At that speed, even a small bolt can smash through a satellite like a cannonball. The International Space Station sometimes has to move out of the way to avoid dangerous pieces. Scientists worry that one day, collisions could create so much debris that parts of space become too dangerous to use. This chain reaction even has a name: the Kessler syndrome.

Why should we care? Satellites help with weather forecasts, maps on our phones, television and the internet. If they are destroyed, many things we rely on every day could stop working. Engineers are now testing clever ways to clean up space. Some ideas include giant nets, magnetic arms and even harpoons to catch old satellites and pull them down, so that they burn up in the atmosphere.

Countries have also agreed on rules to help. New satellites should be designed to fall back towards Earth and burn up once their jobs are done. Just as we shouldn't litter on the beach, we shouldn't litter in space. Space may be enormous, but the part of it that we use is surprisingly crowded. If we look after it now, future astronauts, scientists and maybe even you will be able to explore it safely. The sky is no longer the limit, but it still needs protecting.

title: Every Child Should Learn to Swim
passage: South Africa has beautiful beaches, rivers, dams and thousands of backyard pools. Every summer, families flock to the water to cool off and have fun. Yet every year, too many children drown, often in places they know well, like a pool at home or at a friend's house. In my opinion, learning to swim should be as important as learning to read.

Firstly, swimming saves lives. Drowning is one of the leading causes of accidental death among young children in our country. It is also frighteningly quick and quiet. A child who is drowning usually cannot shout or wave for help. Children who have had proper swimming lessons are far more likely to stay calm, float and reach safety if they fall into the water.

Secondly, swimming is one of the healthiest sports there is. It works almost every muscle in your body, while the water supports your weight and protects your joints. It strengthens your heart and lungs and improves your fitness. Unlike some sports, you can keep swimming your whole life, from toddler to grandparent.

Thirdly, swimming opens the door to many other adventures. If you can swim confidently, you can learn to surf, snorkel, sail or paddle a canoe. You can join a lifesaving club, where you learn to rescue others. Some of the proudest moments in South African sport have happened in the pool, where our swimmers have won Olympic gold medals.

Of course, learning to swim is not a guarantee against danger. Children should always be supervised near water, pools should be fenced, and everyone should swim only in safe areas with lifeguards. But lessons are one of the most powerful tools we have. Some municipalities and clubs offer free or low-cost lessons in summer. So, if you cannot swim yet, ask a parent or teacher to help you find a class. It could be the most important thing you ever learn. And it might just be the most fun as well!

title: The Problem with Plastic
passage: Plastic is everywhere. It wraps our food, holds our drinks, and is used to make toys, clothes and phones. It is cheap, light and strong, which makes it very useful. But the very things that make plastic so useful also make it a serious problem for our planet.

Most plastic takes hundreds of years to break down. Even then, it doesn't disappear. Instead, it crumbles into tiny pieces called microplastics, which are smaller than a grain of rice. Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the ocean, washed there by rivers, stormwater drains and the wind. Scientists have found microplastics everywhere they have looked, from the deepest ocean trenches to the snow on mountain tops.

Sea animals suffer the most. Turtles mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, one of their favourite foods. Seabirds feed bottle caps to their chicks, thinking they are fish. Seals and dolphins get tangled in old fishing nets and cannot swim to the surface to breathe. Along the South African coast, volunteers regularly find animals caught in plastic during beach clean-ups.

The good news is that we can all be part of the solution. The simplest step is to use less plastic in the first place. Carry a reusable water bottle and shopping bag, and say no to plastic straws. When you do use plastic, recycle it properly. Join a beach or river clean-up in your area; even one hour can fill bags with rubbish. You could also encourage your school to start a campaign against single-use plastic.

Some people argue that one person cannot make a difference, because the problem is so enormous. But every piece of plastic you avoid is one less piece that could end up in a turtle's stomach. When millions of people make small changes, big things begin to happen. Several countries, including South Africa, now charge money for plastic shopping bags, and many shops have stopped handing out plastic straws. The ocean gives us food, oxygen and joy. It is time we gave something back.

title: The Mystery of the Mary Celeste
passage: On 4 December 1872, the crew of a ship called the Dei Gratia spotted a strange sight in the Atlantic Ocean. A two-masted ship was drifting slowly across the waves, with nobody at the wheel. It was the Mary Celeste, and what they found on board has puzzled people for more than 150 years.

When sailors from the Dei Gratia climbed aboard, the ship was completely empty. There was no captain, no crew and no passengers. Yet the ship was in fairly good condition, and there was enough food and fresh water for six months. Many of the crew's belongings were still on board. The cargo of more than 1 700 barrels was almost untouched. The only lifeboat, however, was missing.

So what happened to the ten people on board? Over the years, people have suggested all sorts of explanations. Some blamed pirates, but nothing valuable had been stolen. Others imagined sea monsters or giant waves. Many stories were simply invented, including a famous one by the writer Arthur Conan Doyle, who later created the detective Sherlock Holmes.

Today, many historians believe the answer may be less dramatic. The captain's last logbook entry showed that the ship had been near the Azores islands. One theory is that fumes leaked from the barrels, and the captain feared an explosion. Another is that a pump was broken, and he thought the ship was sinking. Either way, he may have ordered everyone into the lifeboat to wait at a safe distance. If the lifeboat's rope snapped, the ship could have sailed away without them. Sadly, the lifeboat and its passengers were never seen again.

We may never know for certain what happened. That is what makes the Mary Celeste such a gripping mystery. It reminds us that even with clues, some questions have no final answer. Good detectives, like good historians, look carefully at the evidence and avoid jumping to conclusions. Which explanation do you think makes the most sense?

title: Your Body's Defence Force
passage: Every day, your body is under attack. Germs such as bacteria and viruses are all around us: in the air, on door handles and on our hands. Most of the time we don't even notice, because our bodies have an amazing defence force called the immune system.

The immune system is made up of special white blood cells that patrol your body, looking for invaders. When they find a germ, some of them make antibodies. Antibodies are a little like keys that fit onto one particular germ and help to destroy it. After the battle, some of these cells remember the germ. If the same germ attacks again, the body recognises it and fights back so fast that you may not get sick at all.

The problem is that the first time you meet a dangerous germ, your body needs time to learn how to fight it. During that time, you can become very ill. This is where vaccines help. A vaccine gives your immune system a safe preview of a germ, using a weakened or harmless version of it, or just a small piece of it. Your body practises making antibodies without you having to catch the real disease.

Vaccines have saved millions of lives. Smallpox, a disease that killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries, has been completely wiped out thanks to vaccination. Polio, which once left many children unable to walk, has almost disappeared. When most people in a community are vaccinated, it is hard for a germ to spread, which also protects babies and people who are too sick to be vaccinated.

Like all medicines, vaccines are tested carefully before they are used, and doctors keep checking them afterwards. Some people feel a sore arm or a slight fever for a day or two, which is a sign that the immune system is doing its job. If you have questions about a vaccine, a nurse or doctor is the best person to ask. Your immune system is a remarkable team of defenders, and vaccines are simply a way of giving it a head start.

title: Why Board Games Are Good for Your Brain
passage: In a world of video games and streaming, board games might seem old-fashioned. After all, people have been playing them for thousands of years. One of the oldest known board games, called Senet, was played in ancient Egypt more than 5 000 years ago. Yet board games are making a comeback, and scientists say that is good news for our brains.

Firstly, board games make us think ahead. In games like chess, draughts or morabaraba, you have to plan several moves in advance and imagine what your opponent might do. This kind of planning strengthens the parts of the brain we use for solving problems and making decisions. Games with dice and pretend money also give us plenty of practice with mental maths.

Secondly, board games teach us how to win and lose gracefully. When you land on the wrong square or your plan fails, you have to stay calm and try again. Learning to congratulate the winner, even when you are disappointed, is an important life skill. Many games also require teamwork, patience and waiting for your turn, which are not always easy!

Thirdly, board games bring people together. Unlike many screen games, they are played face to face. Families and friends sit around the same table, laugh, argue and chat. Grandparents and grandchildren can play together, even if they have very different interests. Morabaraba, for example, has been passed down through many generations in Southern Africa, often scratched into the ground or carved into rock.

Of course, video games can also be fun and can even teach useful skills. The point is not that one is good and the other is bad, but that variety is healthy for our minds. So, the next time it is raining or the power goes off, dig out an old board game instead of sighing with boredom. You might discover that the best game in the house has been sitting in the cupboard all along. You may also find yourself thinking more sharply, laughing more loudly and getting to know your family a little better.

title: Die geheim van die potlood
passage: Byna elke kind in Suid-Afrika het 'n potlood in sy skooltas. Ons gebruik dit om te skryf, te teken en somme te maak. Maar het jy al ooit gewonder hoe die donker "lood" binne-in die hout kom?

In die fabriek word die grafiet fyngemaal en met klei en water gemeng. Hoe meer klei by die mengsel gevoeg word, hoe harder en ligter is die potlood se punt. Die mengsel word in lang, dun stafies gedruk en in 'n baie warm oond gebak.

Intussen word hout, dikwels van seder- of dennebome, in dun plankies gesaag. Masjiene sny klein groefies in die plankies. Die grafietstafies word in die groefies gelê, en 'n tweede plankie word bo-op vasgeplak, soos 'n toebroodjie. Daarna word die "toebroodjie" in afsonderlike potlode gesny en glad geskaaf. Laastens word die potlode geverf, en party kry 'n uitveër aan die een kant.

'n Enkele potlood kan 'n lyn van omtrent vyftig kilometer trek voordat dit opgebruik is! Dit kan ook onderstebo skryf en is selfs al in die ruimte gebruik. Die volgende keer wat jy jou potlood skerp maak, dink aan die lang reis wat dit afgelê het: van die myn na die fabriek, en uiteindelik na jou klaskamer.

title: Up, Up and Away
passage: Early one morning, Ruby and her parents drove to a wide, open field in the Magaliesberg. They had come to take a ride in a hot-air balloon. In the grey light, the huge, colourful balloon lay flat on the grass like a sleeping giant.

"Hot air is lighter than cold air," explained the pilot. "When the air inside the balloon is hotter than the air outside, the balloon floats upwards, just like a bubble rising in water." Ruby held on tightly as the basket lifted off the ground. It was surprisingly quiet and smooth. Below them, the fields looked like a patchwork quilt, and the cows looked as small as ants. They floated over a river, where a heron was fishing, and waved at a farmer on his tractor.

title: Lees is jou superkrag
passage: In 'n wêreld vol skerms, video's en speletjies vra baie kinders: "Hoekom moet ek nog boeke lees?" Dit is 'n goeie vraag. Die antwoord is eenvoudig, maar verrassend: om gereeld te lees, is een van die kragtigste dinge wat jy vir jou brein kan doen.

Wanneer jy lees, werk jou brein harder as wanneer jy na 'n video kyk. Jy moet die woorde ontsyfer, prentjies in jou kop skep en onthou wat vroeër in die storie gebeur het. Navorsers het gevind dat kinders wat elke dag lees, beter konsentreer en 'n groter woordeskat het. Met elke boek leer jy honderde nuwe woorde sonder dat jy dit eers agterkom.

Lees help jou ook in elke skoolvak. Om 'n wiskundeprobleem op te los, moet jy eers die vraag verstaan. In wetenskap, geskiedenis en geografie lees jy om nuwe inligting te leer. Kinders wat vlot lees, vind dus dikwels al hul vakke makliker. Hulle skryf ook beter, want hulle het gesien hoe goeie skrywers sinne bou.

Maar lees is nie net vir punte nie. 'n Boek kan jou na plekke neem wat jy nog nooit gesien het nie: die diepte van die see, 'n kasteel in die wolke of 'n dorpie aan die ander kant van die wêreld. Wanneer jy lees oor karakters wat anders is as jy, leer jy om te verstaan hoe ander mense voel. Wetenskaplikes noem dit empatie. Lees kan jou ook help om te ontspan en rustig te raak na 'n besige dag.

Hoe word jy 'n leser? Begin met boeke oor dinge waarvan jy hou, of dit nou dinosourusse, sokker of towerstories is. Lees elke dag, al is dit net tien minute voor jy gaan slaap. Besoek die biblioteek, ruil boeke met jou maats, of lees saam met 'n boetie of sussie. Moenie bekommerd wees as jy stadig lees nie; hoe meer jy oefen, hoe vinniger en makliker word dit. Jy hoef nie 'n kapmantel te dra om 'n superheld te wees nie. Soms is 'n goeie boek al die superkrag wat jy nodig het.

title: Die Groot Migrasie
passage: Elke jaar vind een van die grootste natuurwonders op aarde in Oos-Afrika plaas. Meer as een miljoen wildebeeste, saam met honderdduisende sebras en gazelles, trek in 'n reuse sirkel deur Tanzanië en Kenia. Die troppe is so groot dat 'n mens hulle selfs van 'n vliegtuig af kan sien. Hierdie reis word die Groot Migrasie genoem.

Die diere volg die reën. Wanneer die grasvlaktes van die Serengeti in Tanzanië opdroog, trek die troppe noord op soek na vars gras. Hulle reis honderde kilometers en bereik teen die middel van die jaar die Masai Mara in Kenia. Wanneer die reën later weer in die suide val, keer hulle terug. Die hele reis duur 'n jaar en herhaal elke jaar.

Die gevaarlikste deel van die reis is die oorsteek van die Mararivier. Die water vloei vinnig, en die walle is steil en glad. In die rivier wag groot krokodille, en op die oewer lê leeus en ander roofdiere en wag. Duisende wildebeeste huiwer by die water, totdat een dapper dier spring en die res blindelings volg. Ongelukkig haal nie almal die oorkant nie.

Tog is die migrasie 'n wonderlike voorbeeld van hoe die natuur in balans bly. Die groot troppe bemes die grond, wat nuwe gras laat groei. Die karkasse van diere wat sterf, voed aasvoëls, hiënas en selfs visse in die rivier. Omtrent 'n halwe miljoen kalwers word elke jaar gebore, gewoonlik binne 'n paar weke van mekaar. Omdat daar so baie gelyk gebore word, kan roofdiere nie almal vang nie.

Vandag besoek toeriste van oor die hele wêreld die gebied om hierdie skouspel met hul eie oë te sien. Maar die migrasie is kwesbaar. Heinings, paaie en plase kan die diere se roete versper, en droogtes word erger. Natuurbewaarders werk hard om die groot vlaktes oop te hou, sodat die diere vry kan beweeg. As hulle daarin slaag, sal ons kleinkinders eendag ook kan sien hoe die aarde bewe onder miljoene hoewe. Dit is 'n skouspel wat die moeite werd is om te beskerm.

title: Van skaduwee tot atoomhorlosie
passage: Vandag kyk ons net na ons foon of horlosie om te weet hoe laat dit is. Maar vir duisende jare het mense geen horlosies gehad nie. Tog het hulle slim maniere gevind om die tyd te meet.

Die eerste "horlosie" was die son self. Mense het opgelet dat skaduwees gedurende die dag van rigting en lengte verander. Die ou Egiptenare het meer as drieduisend jaar gelede sonwysers gebou. 'n Sonwyser het 'n regop pen wat 'n skaduwee op 'n plat skyf met merke gooi. Soos die son oor die lug beweeg, skuif die skaduwee van merk tot merk. Die probleem was natuurlik dat sonwysers snags of op bewolkte dae nutteloos was.

Daarom het mense ander uitvindings gemaak. 'n Waterhorlosie was 'n bak met 'n klein gaatjie onder in. Die water het stadig uitgedrup, en merke aan die kant het gewys hoeveel tyd verby is. Later het mense uurglase gebruik, waarin fyn sand van een glas na 'n ander deur 'n smal nek loop. In party lande het mense selfs kerse met merke laat brand om die ure te tel.

Die eerste meganiese horlosies is omtrent sewehonderd jaar gelede in Europa gebou. Hulle was so groot dat hulle in kerktorings geplaas is, en baie het nie eens 'n minuutwyser gehad nie. Mettertyd het horlosiemakers hulle kleiner en akkurater gemaak, totdat mense hulle in hul sakke kon dra. Vandag meet atoomhorlosies die tyd so akkuraat dat hulle in miljoene jare skaars een sekonde fouteer. Hulle help selfs die GPS in ons fone om ons presies te vind.

Dit is verbasend om te dink hoe ver ons gekom het, van 'n stok in die sand tot 'n horlosie wat die trillings van atome tel. Tog is die basiese idee nog dieselfde: ons soek iets wat op 'n gereelde manier verander, en ons tel dit. Die volgende keer wat jy vra hoe laat dit is, onthou die slim uitvinders wat dit vir ons moontlik gemaak het. Dalk sal jy eendag self die volgende groot uitvinding maak!

title: Speak a New Language, See a New World
passage: South Africa has twelve official languages, including South African Sign Language. Yet many of us can speak only one or two of them. In my opinion, every child should learn at least one more language, and the earlier, the better.

Firstly, learning a language is excellent exercise for the brain. When you switch between languages, your brain has to decide which words to use and which to ignore. Researchers have found that people who speak more than one language are often good at solving problems and paying attention. Children's brains are especially good at picking up new sounds, which is why young learners often develop better accents.

Secondly, languages open doors to friendship. Imagine greeting a new classmate in their home language: "Sawubona", "Dumela" or "Molo". Their face would light up! When we make the effort to speak someone else's language, we show them respect. In a country with so many cultures, this can help to build understanding between people.

Thirdly, knowing more languages can help you in the future. Many jobs, especially in tourism, medicine and business, need people who can speak to others in their own language. A nurse who can speak isiZulu, Afrikaans and English, for example, can comfort many more patients. Languages also make travelling more fun, because you can chat to local people, read menus and understand signs.

Some people argue that learning a new language is too difficult or takes too much time. It is true that it requires patience, and you will make mistakes. But nobody expects you to be perfect at the start. Learn a few words every day, listen to songs and watch programmes in the new language, and practise with friends who speak it. Little by little, the words will start to make sense. A famous saying tells us that a different language is a different way of seeing life. Why not start seeing the world in a new way today?

title: The Songs of the Humpback Whale
passage: Every winter, thousands of humpback whales swim past the coast of South Africa. They travel from the icy waters of Antarctica, where they feed in summer, to warmer waters further north, where they give birth. Their journey is one of the longest migrations of any mammal on Earth.

Humpback whales are enormous. An adult can be as long as a bus and weigh as much as several elephants. Yet they feed on some of the smallest animals in the sea: tiny, shrimp-like creatures called krill. To catch them, a group of whales sometimes swims in a circle below a shoal, blowing bubbles to form a "net". Then they rise through the middle with their mouths wide open.

The most amazing thing about humpbacks, however, is their singing. Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs made of moans, squeaks and deep rumbles. A single song can last for up to twenty minutes, and a whale may repeat it for hours. The sound can travel for kilometres through the water. Scientists believe the songs may help males to attract females, but nobody knows for certain.

Even more remarkably, all the males in one area sing the same song. Over time, the song slowly changes, and every whale changes it in the same way. Sometimes a completely new song spreads from one ocean region to another, like a hit song on the radio. This shows that whales can learn from one another, which is very rare in the animal world.

Not long ago, humpback whales were in serious trouble. Hunters killed so many that they almost disappeared. After whaling was banned, their numbers slowly grew again. Today, you can often see them from the shore or on a boat trip along the coasts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape. If you are lucky, you might even see one leap right out of the water. And if you could put your head underwater, you might just hear one singing.

title: The Race to the South Pole
passage: In 1911, two teams of explorers set out on a dangerous race. Both wanted to be the first people ever to reach the South Pole, the coldest and loneliest place on Earth. One team was led by Roald Amundsen from Norway. The other was led by Robert Falcon Scott from Britain.

The two leaders planned their journeys very differently. Amundsen had learnt from the Inuit people of the Arctic. His team wore warm clothes made of animal fur and travelled on skis, with sledges pulled by dogs. Scott relied partly on motor sledges and ponies, but the engines broke down in the cold, and the ponies struggled in the snow. In the end, Scott's men had to pull their heavy sledges themselves.

Amundsen's team moved quickly across the ice. On 14 December 1911, they reached the South Pole and planted the Norwegian flag. They left a tent there, with a letter for Scott inside. Then they turned around and made it safely back to their base.

Scott's team arrived at the Pole about five weeks later, on 17 January 1912. When they saw the Norwegian flag flapping in the wind, they were heartbroken. The journey back was terrible. Blizzards raged, food ran short and temperatures dropped below minus forty degrees Celsius. Sadly, Scott and his four companions never made it home.

Today, both men are remembered for their courage. Scott's diaries, found months later, showed how bravely his team had faced their fate. Amundsen's success showed the value of careful planning and of learning from people who already know how to survive in harsh places. A research station now stands at the South Pole, named after both explorers: the Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station. The race is long over, but its lessons about preparation, teamwork and bravery are still important today.
